title: The Bridge Is Not a Metaphor
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 41 · Lanternweald continuation
content:
The trouble with an ordinary bridge was that everyone understood the word *bridge* until somebody asked who could cross it.

The trouble with our household was that three very powerful people believed they understood an ordinary bridge better than anyone else.

“I can move the entire thing,” Toph announced.

“You absolutely cannot,” Katara said.

“Watch me.”

“No.”

Aang put his hand between them in the patient gesture that usually meant he was about to make the situation worse by trying to improve it.

“What if we started with the people who use it?”

I raised my pencil.

“Finally,” I said. “A sentence worth writing down.”

We were standing above Riverstone Terrace, where the new public path crossed a narrow drainage channel before reaching Lanternwell Square. During the night, Threadrain had softened the earth under the western support. The bridge had not collapsed. It had only sunk enough that the narrow entry lip became a step, and the flat walkway leaned toward its railing.

Someone had set a temporary sign on the path.

CLOSED FOR YOUR SAFETY.

This was accurate. It was also useless to anyone who needed to reach the other side.

A produce vendor named Sella stood beside her handcart, looking at the bridge as though she could make it behave by being furious. Beside her waited a neighbor who used a wheeled chair, with a basket of flour balanced on their lap. They had come from the community bakery.

“There's another route,” an official told them.

“An hour out of the way,” Sella replied.

“Only forty minutes.”

“Forgive me. Obviously that makes it fine.”

Toph planted one foot against the ground. “The west support is moving. Nobody should be on it until we brace it.”

“I agree,” I said.

She tilted her head toward me. “That sounded painful.”

“I can agree with you and still ask how we get people across.”

Aang was already looking at the detour map. He could carry three people by air in less than a minute. He offered.

The baker thanked him and declined.

“I don't want to owe a ride from the Avatar every time I need flour,” they said.

That stopped him.

I could see it happening. Aang's instinct was to help. He was good at helping. Sometimes he had to be reminded that being able to carry a person did not make carrying them a public transportation policy.

“We need another path,” Katara said.

“We need a proper footing,” Toph corrected.

“We need both,” I said.

The official stared at my notebook. “You can write a request for temporary funding.”

“I can write six requests,” I said. “The bridge will still be crooked.”

Sella snorted.

That was how our morning began.

It became more interesting when Danse arrived from Brasswatch Yard carrying a box of bolts and the expression of a man who had been told the problem could be solved with bolts.

I had warned him Toph was coming.

I had not warned Toph about him.

“You the engineer?” she asked.

“I've repaired field structures under worse conditions.”

“Great. Then you know to keep your boots off the soft side.”

He stopped midstep.

“I'm aware of the risk.”

“You were about to step there.”

Danse looked at the ground, then at me. I looked at my notebook. I had no intention of rescuing either of them from an accurate observation.

“What do you propose?” he asked.

Toph placed her foot against the stone. “The south bank isn't shifting. We anchor there, widen the support, and rebuild the approach.”

“Your materials won't handle repeated loads without bracing.”

“Then brace them.”

“That's what I was trying to say.”

“Then you're doing great.”

I heard Aang make a noise suspiciously like a laugh behind me.

Danse did not look amused.

Not until Toph tapped the edge of the failing support and a hairline crack appeared beneath the bolt he had been about to tighten.

He crouched to inspect it.

“Good catch,” he said.

She shrugged. “Good eyes.”

I nearly dropped my pencil.

By midday we had a plan. It was not Toph's alone or Danse's alone. They had worked through the load, the drainage, the railing, and the difference between a temporary walkway and a rebuilt one. Sella had pointed out that the approach needed space for turning a loaded cart. The baker had insisted the surface remain level across the join. Katara secured a safe crossing schedule for medicine and urgent supplies until the repair was finished.

Aang helped carry materials only after someone asked him.

That last detail made me unreasonably proud.

At lunch we ate on the steps outside the community room. The meal was bread, lentils, and whatever Toph had stolen from Aang's plate.

“Shared household resources,” she said.

“It's my lunch.”

“Your lunch has excellent taste.”

Katara leaned across me and took back the bread.

“Ask.”

Toph groaned. “This family has too many rules.”

“You signed the rules,” I said.

“I was young.”

“Last year,” Aang reminded her.

“Ancient history.”

The familiar joke steadied me. It had been a long morning of people thanking us for fixing a problem we had not yet fixed. Sometimes the gratitude felt like permission to stop thinking. We couldn't afford that.

After lunch, Aang stayed behind to speak with the officials. Katara returned to the clinic with the baker. Toph went back to the bridge because she did not trust anybody else to notice the foundation shifting.

I found ten minutes alone on the terrace, or thought I did, until Katara appeared with two cups of tea.

“Your handwriting is getting worse,” she said.

“That's the most romantic thing you've ever told me.”

“Good. I've been saving it.”

She handed me a cup and sat beside me on the low wall.

“Are we going to talk about tonight?” she asked.

I knew what she meant. I'd planned to meet someone through the Moonroot Door for a promised conversation and had forgotten to tell them which evening I would be home.

“I meant to bring it up at breakfast.”

“Then breakfast would have been a good time.”

“I know.”

Katara was quiet for a moment. She did not need a speech about how ethical non-monogamy worked. We'd already had the discussions. She needed the behavior that made the words real.

“I don't mind you going,” she said. “I mind finding out from the calendar after I've arranged dinner.”

“That's fair. I should have asked about the plan before I made another one.”

“Will you?”

“Yes.”

She rested her shoulder against mine.

“We don't need to agree on every choice,” she said. “But I would like to know which choices affect the house.”

“I can do that.”

“You can also stop volunteering to become every district's secretary.”

“Toph would miss the opportunity to insult my handwriting.”

“Toph can survive disappointment.”

I turned my face toward hers.

“May I kiss you?”

Katara's eyes warmed. “You've been helpful all day. I suppose.”

I kissed her slowly, tasting tea on her lips, and she caught the front of my jacket before I could pull away.

“That,” she said, “was not an apology.”

“No.”

“Good. Do the apology too.”

“I'm sorry I left you to guess what the evening would look like.”

She kissed my cheek. “Accepted.”

We sat together until the work bell rang.

The repair took three more days. Nobody died. No one made a heroic speech. Danse and Toph argued about a brace before discovering they were arguing about two different braces. Aang wore himself out carrying gravel and learned to take a rest without being ordered. Katara kept the clinic open to visitors who used the detour.

On the fourth morning, the baker rolled across the new bridge with flour in their lap.

They stopped in the center, tested the surface, and continued without asking anyone for help.

Sella followed with her cart.

Toph stood beside me, arms folded. “Perfect.”

“You'd say that even if it wasn't.”

“No,” she said. “If it wasn't, I'd be louder.”

Across the channel, Danse was tightening the last railing bracket while Aang held a bucket of bolts and Katara distributed water to the workers.

I looked at the bridge.

It was strong because different people had been allowed to describe the same problem truthfully.

That thought was almost annoyingly symbolic.

I decided not to tell Toph.

She grinned.

“You're thinking about metaphors again.”

“I am not.”

“Liar.”

Aang waved from the far side. Katara lifted a cup in greeting. The path lay open between us, and for once nobody needed to carry anybody across.

I put my notebook away and went to join them.
